title: The Berlin Bear - FAQ
subtitle: Why the city has a bear, and where to see the ones worth finding.

items.q: Why is the bear the symbol of Berlin?
items.a: Because of the name. Berlin is most likely a Slavic name meaning swamp or wet ground, but it sounds like **Bär**, the German word for bear. Medieval towns liked arms that played on their own name, so Berlin took a bear.

items.q: When did the bear first appear on Berlin's coat of arms?
items.a: On the city seal of **1280**, where two bears stand beside the shield with the Brandenburg eagle. The older seal of 1253 shows only the eagle. The bear became the main figure in the 14th and 15th centuries.

items.q: Did Berlin really keep live bears in the city centre?
items.a: Yes. The **Bärenzwinger** in Köllnischer Park housed brown bears from **1939 to 2015**. The last one, Schnute, died in October 2015. The building is now a free art space, open daily from 10:00 to 18:00.

items.q: Where can I see Knut the polar bear?
items.a: Knut's mounted body is in the **Museum für Naturkunde** on Invalidenstraße 43. The museum is closed on Mondays and needs a ticket; book a time slot online.

items.q: What are the Buddy Bears in Berlin?
items.a: Painted life-size bear sculptures with raised arms, started by **Eva and Klaus Herlitz** with the sculptor Roman Strobl in the early 2000s. Hotels, embassies and companies own them, so they stand all over the city.

items.q: Is the Berlinale bear the same as the Berlin bear?
items.a: Not quite. The Golden and Silver Bears are small versions of the **Berliner Bär by Renée Sintenis**, a young bear with a raised paw. A large bronze of the same bear stands on the A115 motorway at Dreilinden.
